Running an application with Docker Compose
Once our images are i d x _ 5 5 d 0 5 c 8 1 built, the next step is to bring the entire i d x _ 0 d f f 7 7 4 c application to life. With a single command, Docker
Compose will create the required networks, volumes, and containers, and run all services exactly as we defined
them in our Compose file.
We can start the application using Docker Compose:
$ docker compose up
The output, similar to the output we discussed in the previous section for the db and pgadmin services, will look as
follows for the web service:
web-1 |
web-1 | > wild-animals@2.0.0 start
web-1 | > node src/server.js
web-1 |
web-1 | DB_HOST: db
web-1 | Application listening on port 3000
This indicates that the containerized web service is ready and is listening on port 3000. Coincidentally, we have
mapped container port 3000 to the same port 3000 on the host in our compose.yml file. Thus, we can just open a
355 Managing Containers with Docker Compose
new browser tab and navigate to the URL http://localhost:3000/animal; we should once again see a wild animal
displayed.
Click the Refresh button a few times to see other animal images. The application selects the current image
randomly from a set of 12 images whose URLs are stored in the database.
As the application is running in interactive mode and, thus, the terminal where we ran Docker Compose is blocked,
we can cancel the application by pressing Ctrl + C. If we do so, we will see the following:
Figure 11.19: Stopping the application of step-2
We will notice that the db and web services stop immediately. Sometimes, though, some services will take about 10
seconds to do so. The reason for this is that the db and the web service listen and react to the SIGTERM signal sent by
Docker, while other services might not, and so Docker kills them after a predefined timeout interval of 10 seconds.
If we run the application again with docker compose up, the startup will be much faster, as the database doesn't
have to initialize from scratch, but just reuses the data that was already present in the pg-data volume from the
previous run.
We can also run the application in the background. All containers will run as daemons. For this, we just need to use

Why is there a step-2 prefix in the name of the volume? In the compose.yml file, we have called the volumes to use
pg-data and pgadmin-data. But, as we have already mentioned, Docker Compose prefixes all names with the name
of the parent folder of the compose.yml file plus an i d x _ f 1 2 5 0 2 3 9 underscore. In i d x _ 4 a 6 4 e d c c this case, the parent folder is called step-2. If you
don't like this approach, you can define a project name explicitly, for example, as follows:
$ docker compose --project-name demo up --detach

This way, all resources (containers, networks, and volumes) will be prefixed by the project name – in this case,

Scaling a service
Now, let's, for a moment, assume that i d x _ 8 4 2 b 1 0 1 9 our sample application has been live on the web and become very successful.
Loads of people want to see our cute animal images. But now we're facing a problem: our application has started to
slow down. To overcome this problem, we want to run multiple instances of the web service. With Docker
Compose, this is readily done.
Running more instances is also called scaling out. We can use this tool to scale our web service up to, say, three
instances:
$ docker compose up --scale web=3
Compose creates multiple containers for the same service. The containers are named web-1, web-2, and web-3.
If we do this, we are in for a surprise. The output will look as in the following screenshot:
357 Managing Containers with Docker Compose
Figure 11.22 – Output of docker compose --scale
The second and third instances of the web service fail to start. The error message tells us why we cannot use the
same host port, 3000, more than once. When instances 2 and 3 try to start, Docker realizes that port 3000 is already
taken by the first instance. What can we do? Well, we can just let Docker decide which i d x _ 4 9 9 2 2 c 9 d host port to use for each
instance.
If, in the ports section of the Docker Compose file, we only specify the container port and leave out the host port,
then Docker automatically selects an ephemeral port. Let's do exactly this:
First, let's tear down the application (if it is still running). While still in the step-2 folder, run this
command:
$ docker compose down -v
Then, navigate to the chapter's folder (chapter-11):
$ cd ~/The-Ultimate-Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition

Overrides can become a bit cumbersome to use, specifically in applications with many services and many
i d x _ 3 2 e 0 1 4 e 3 environments. There is finally a better way (in most cases), namely the use of the include statement. Let's look at
this next.
Modularizing applications with include
In larger projects, it i d x _ a 5 c a 7 8 8 c quickly becomes cumbersome to maintain a i d x _ b 6 e a 5 9 9 6 single, ever-growing Docker Compose file. Teams
often want to split configuration into multiple files and keep service definitions close to the code they belong to.
Until recently, the only way to achieve this was by chaining multiple files together with the -f parameter or by
relying on overrides.
Since Docker Compose v2.20, a new top-level key called include allows us to modularize our Compose
configuration in a clean and robust way.
With include, you can point to one or more Compose files, and Docker Compose will merge them into the current
project. Each included file is evaluated in the context of its own project directory. This means that relative paths for
build contexts, volume mounts, or env_file references are resolved correctly, just as if the file were run on its own.
The short form looks like this:
include:
- ../services/db/compose.yaml
- ../services/web/compose.yaml
Had we followed the standard naming convention and called the base file just compose.yml and the
override file compose.override.yml instead, then we could have started the application with docker
compose up -d without explicitly naming the Docker Compose files. In any other case, we need to use the
following full and more verbose syntax:
$ docker compose -f <base compose file> -f <override compose file> up
Tip
In short: include ≠ overrides. Overrides merge/override fields of the same service definition; include lets
you pull in entire Compose files (and you'll get an error on name clashes instead of a silent merge).
Note
365 Managing Containers with Docker Compose
There is also a long form with more control:
include:
- path: ../services/db/compose.yaml
project_directory: ../services/db
env_file:
- ../services/db/.env
This allows you to i d x _ 6 8 b 2 0 4 f 7 override where relative paths are i d x _ 9 a 4 6 2 c 5 f resolved and which environment files should be considered for
variable substitution.
You can even nest includes recursively, which makes this feature ideal for large monorepos or cross-team setups
where each team owns its own Compose file. A top-level file can simply include all relevant modules and start the
full stack with a single docker compose up command.

chunks.heading: Chapter 11 368
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 368
Intentional conflicts (what not to do): If two include entries (or an include and the root file) define a
resource with the same name (for example, both define a catalog service), Compose errors out rather
than silently merging. This is by design, so each module can stay independent and predictable. Rename
the conflicting service or split concerns.
Recursive includes: An included file may itself use include: (for example, services/web/compose.yaml
could include services/web/observability.yaml). Compose resolves these recursively, still honoring
each file's project directory for relative paths. Keep the tree shallow to avoid surprises.
With the include feature, Docker i d x _ a 7 7 d 0 7 0 9 Compose finally gives us a clean i d x _ 6 5 9 e 3 1 a 4 and modular way to assemble complex stacks,
allowing each service to keep its own configuration while still coming together seamlessly into a single application.
When to use Docker Compose versus a full
orchestration system
By now, you have i d x _ c a a 0 4 f f 0 seen how Docker Compose makes it easy to define, build, and run multi-service applications on a
single host. For developers and continuous integration systems, this is often all you need: fast startup, repeatable
environments, and the ability to scale out a service for quick testing. Compose shines in local development,
automated pipelines, demos, and simple deployments where you do not need clustering or advanced scheduling.
But there comes a point where Docker Compose reaches its natural limits. If you want to run your application
across multiple nodes, ensure high availability, perform rolling upgrades without downtime, or manage hundreds
of services in production, you need a full orchestration system. Tools such as Docker Swarm or Kubernetes take the
declarative idea you learned here and extend it to an entire cluster. They keep your applications in the desired state
even in the face of node i d x _ 9 f 4 f d d a d failures, scaling demands, and complex networking.
Following is a concise comparison table:

Kubernetes)

5.6 In short
Use Docker Compose when you are working on a single host, testing, or running simple stacks; use an
orchestrator when you must run containerized applications reliably in production at scale. In Chapter 14,
Introducing Container Orchestration, we will take this step and look at how orchestration systems build
upon the very foundation we have laid here with Compose.

With Docker Compose, we have a simple yet powerful tool for local development and small-scale deployments,
while orchestration systems take over once we need to manage containerized applications across clusters with
resilience and scale.
Compose has given i d x _ 4 3 7 e e 2 8 2 us the foundation to define and run multi-service applications with ease; in the next chapters,
we will build on this foundation and see how orchestrators and monitoring complete the picture for running
containers in production.
Summary
In this chapter, we saw how Docker Compose lets us define, build, and run multi-service applications on a single
Docker host with just a few commands. Instead of starting containers manually, Compose allows us to declare our
desired application state in a YAML file and let Docker take care of the rest. We learned how to build images, run
applications, scale services, and adapt configurations with overrides.
We also looked at important recent changes: Compose V2 is now part of the Docker CLI, BuildKit powers faster and
more secure builds, and the new include keyword enables us to split large Compose setups into modular building
blocks. Together, these improvements make Compose a more flexible and developer-friendly tool than ever before.
With Docker Compose, we now have a simple yet powerful way to manage applications consisting of multiple
containers on a single host.
In the next chapter, we are going to introduce orchestrators. An orchestrator is infrastructure software that is used
to run and manage containerized applications in a cluster while making sure that these applications are in their
desired state at all times.

In an imperative approach, we tell the system step by step what to do and how to react to unexpected

Chapter 11 376
12
Shipping Logs and Monitoring
Containers
In the previous chapter, we introduced Docker Compose, a powerful tool for defining and running multi-container
applications on a single Docker host. We learned that Compose files use a declarative YAML format and are ideal
for developers and CI servers that need to coordinate several containers together. We also explored practical tasks
such as building and pushing images and running complete application stacks locally.
In this chapter, we move from running containers to understanding and operating them. We will explore why
logging and monitoring are essential in any containerized environment and how to implement both effectively.
You will learn how to collect, ship, and visualize logs and how to instrument your applications to expose metrics
that describe their health and performance.
We begin by examining Docker's native logging capabilities and the importance of log rotation and retention. You
will then learn how to ship container and Docker daemon logs to a central location using the Elastic Stack,
specifically Filebeat, Elasticsearch, and Kibana.
On Linux, Filebeat can read container logs directly from /var/lib/docker/containers. Docker stores container
logs in JSON format under /var/lib/docker/containers/<container-id>/. Each container has its own log file
that can be collected by logging agents.
On macOS and Windows, where Docker runs inside a lightweight VM, we use a practical workaround: applications
write their logs into a shared volume, and Filebeat tails those files to forward them to Elasticsearch. This approach
mirrors what you learned earlier in the book for cross-platform log shipping and makes the examples work
seamlessly on all operating systems.
After centralizing logs, we'll use Kibana to search, filter, and visualize them, learning how to enrich log events with
helpful metadata such as service.name. Next, we'll turn to Prometheus, the most popular open source monitoring
and alerting system, to collect quantitative metrics from running containers. You'll build a small demo with three
microservices, written in Go, Python, and C#, to see how easily different languages can expose Prometheus metrics.
Finally, we'll connect Grafana to Prometheus to build dashboards and even add basic alerting.
Finally, we broaden the discussion from logs and metrics to the concept of observability, which also includes
tracing and runtime security monitoring.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to do the following:
Define and configure logging drivers and rotation policies for containers
Collect and ship container and daemon logs to a central Elastic Stack instance
Query, filter, and visualize aggregated logs in Kibana
Expose and scrape application metrics using Prometheus
Build dashboards in Grafana to monitor your containers

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 376
chunks.content:
Understand how observability unifies logs, metrics, and traces, and why security monitoring is part of
modern container operations
Technical requirements
The code accompanying this chapter can be found at https://github.com/PacktPublishing/The-Ultimate-
Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition/tree/main/chapter-12/solutions.
Before we start, let's make sure you have a folder ready for the code you are going to implement in this chapter.
Navigate to the folder where you cloned the code repository that accompanies this book. Normally, this is the ~/
The-Ultimate-Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition folder in your home folder:
$ cd ~/The-Ultimate-Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition
Create a subfolder called chapter-12 and navigate to it:
$ mkdir chapter-12 && cd chapter-12
Platform differences
All examples run natively on Linux. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs the Docker engine inside a
lightweight Linux virtual machine. Because of this abstraction, internal Docker paths such as /var/lib/docker/
containers are not directly accessible from the host system.
Where needed (for example, when shipping container logs), the chapter uses a cross-platform workaround:
containers write their logs to a shared mounted volume, and Filebeat tails the files from that volume. This ensures
that all examples behave consistently, regardless of your operating system.
•
•
•
•
•
•
In earlier versions of this book, we demonstrated log i d x _ 7 e f 0 2 6 4 2 shipping with Elastic Agent. Since Elastic Agent now
i d x _ 4 5 7 7 3 9 4 8 expects Fleet enrollment by default and has become more complex to configure in standalone mode, we
use Filebeat in this i d x _ f a d 8 2 7 0 8 edition instead. Filebeat remains part of the Elastic Stack, is lightweight, and is
perfectly suited for learning how to collect and forward container logs. The examples in this chapter also
follow the cross-platform pattern used earlier in the book for macOS and Windows: applications write
logs into a shared volume that Filebeat reads and ships to Elasticsearch. This approach ensures the hands-
on labs run smoothly on any system.

chunks.heading: Chapter 12 378
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 378
Without further ado, let's dive into the first topic of shipping containers and daemon logs.
Why logging and monitoring matter
When working with a i d x _ 8 3 7 f 4 4 b f distributed mission-critical application in production or any production-like environment, it
is of utmost importance to gain as much insight as possible into the inner workings of those applications. Have you
ever had a chance to investigate the cockpit of an airplane or the command center of a nuclear power plant? Both
an airplane and a power plant are examples of highly complex systems that deliver mission-critical services. If a
plane crashes or a power plant shuts down unexpectedly, a lot of people are negatively affected, to say the least.
Thus, the cockpit and the command center are full of instruments showing the current or past state of some parts
of the system. What you see there is the visual representation of some sensors that are placed in strategic parts of
the system and constantly collect data such as the temperature or the flow rate.
Similar to an airplane or a power plant, our application needs to be instrumented with "sensors" that can feel the
"temperature" of our application services or the infrastructure they run on. I put the word temperature in double
quotes since it is only a placeholder for things that matter in an application, such as the number of requests per
second on a given RESTful endpoint, or the average latency of requests to the same endpoint.
The resulting values or readings that we collect, such as the average latency of requests, are often called metrics. It i d x _ 8 9 4 1 b 9 a d
should be our goal to expose as many meaningful metrics as possible of the application services we build. Metrics
can be both functional and non-functional. Functional metrics are values that say something business-relevant
about the application service, such as how many checkouts are performed per minute if the service is part of an e-
commerce application, or which are the five most popular songs over the last 24 hours if we are talking about a
streaming application.
Non-functional metrics are important values that are not specific to the kind of business the application is used for,
such as the average latency of a particular web request, how many 4xx status codes are returned per minute by
another endpoint, or how much RAM or how many CPU cycles a given service is consuming.
In a distributed system where each part is exposing metrics, some overarching service should be collecting and
aggregating the values periodically from each component. Alternatively, each component should forward its
metrics to a central metrics server. Only if the metrics for all components of our highly distributed system are
available for inspection in a central location are they of any value. Otherwise, monitoring the system becomes

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 378
chunks.content:
impossible. That's why pilots of an airplane never have to go and inspect individual and critical parts of the
airplane in person during a flight; all necessary readings are collected and displayed in the cockpit.
Today, one of the most popular services that is used to expose, collect, and store metrics is Prometheus. It is an i d x _ 4 f e c a f d c
open source project and has been donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). Prometheus i d x _ 7 6 c e b e 9 6 has
first-class integration with Docker containers, Kubernetes, and many other systems and programming platforms.
In this chapter, we will use Prometheus i d x _ f 6 c 0 8 d b 8 to demonstrate how to instrument a simple service that exposes important
metrics.
In the next section, we are going to show you how to ship containers and Docker daemon logs to a central location.
379 Shipping Logs and Monitoring Containers
Shipping container logs
In the world of containerization, understanding the logs generated by your Docker i d x _ 4 8 d 8 a c 7 3 environment is crucial for
maintaining a healthy and well-functioning system. This section will provide an overview of two key types of logs
you will encounter: shipping container logs and Docker daemon logs. We i d x _ 9 e 8 b e 7 b a start with the former.
As applications run within containers, they generate log messages that provide valuable insights into their
performance and any potential problems.
Container logs can be accessed using the docker container logs command, followed by the container's ID or
name. These logs can help developers and system administrators diagnose issues, monitor container activities, and
ensure the smooth operation of deployed applications. Centralizing and analyzing container logs is essential for
optimizing resource usage, identifying performance bottlenecks, and troubleshooting application issues.
Some best practices for managing shipping container logs include the following:
Configuring log i d x _ b 9 9 d 4 1 f 1 rotation and retention policies to prevent excessive disk space usage
Using a log management system to centralize logs from multiple containers
Setting up log filtering and alerting mechanisms to identify critical events and anomalies
Let's look at these recommendations in detail, starting with log rotation and retention policies.
Configuring log rotation and retention policies
Configuring log i d x _ c a 4 1 a 9 c 8 rotation and retention policies for container logs is essential for preventing excessive disk space
usage and maintaining optimal performance. Here's a step-by-step guide on how to set up these policies for
Docker container logs.
Configuring the logging driver
Docker supports i d x _ 0 8 6 f d 9 1 a various logging drivers, such as json-file, syslog, journald, and more. To configure the logging

example, we'll use the json-file logging driver, which is the default driver for Docker.
Globally setting the log driver
To set the logging i d x _ b 9 5 d 2 2 0 f driver globally, edit the /etc/docker/daemon.json configuration file (create it if it doesn't exist)
and do the following:

2.3 381 Shipping Logs and Monitoring Containers
Locally setting the log driver
If you prefer to set the i d x _ 1 f 8 4 a a b 8 logging driver for an individual container instead of globally, then use the --log-driver
option when starting the container:
$ docker run --log-driver=json-file <image_name> ...
Now, let's learn how to specify log rotation and retention policies.
Setting log rotation and retention policies
We can configure log rotation and i d x _ d 1 1 1 c f e 3 retention policies by specifying the max-size and max-file options for the
logging driver:
max-size: This option limits the size of each log file. When a log file reaches the specified size, Docker
creates a new file and starts logging to it. For example, to limit each log file to 10 MB, set max-size=10m.
max-file: This option limits the number of log files to keep. When the limit is reached, Docker removes
the oldest log file. For example, to keep only the last five log files, set max-file=5.
To set these options globally, add them to the /etc/docker/daemon.json configuration file. We can add the log-
opts section to the daemon configuration right after the log-driver node that we added earlier:
{
...
"log-driver": "json-file",
"log-opts": {
"max-size": "10m",
"max-file": "5"
}
}
We suggest that you modify the daemon configuration once again via the dashboard of Docker Desktop. Once you
have modified the configuration, restart the Docker daemon to apply the changes.
To set these options for an individual container, use the --log-opt option when starting the container:
$ docker run --log-driver=json-file \
--log-opt max-size=10m \
--log-opt max-file=5 \
<image_name> ...

Chapter 12 382
By configuring log rotation and retention i d x _ 0 5 c d 7 b e 1 policies, you can prevent excessive disk space usage and maintain a well-
functioning Docker environment. Remember to choose appropriate values for max-size and max-file based on
your specific use case and storage capacity.
Using a log management system
So far, we have seen how logs can be collected from containers i d x _ d 5 7 c d 0 d 6 and the Docker daemon. However, logs are only
truly useful when they are centralized, searchable, and visualized. This is where a log management system comes
in. One of the most popular solutions in this space is the Elastic Stack (formerly known as the ELK stack, short for
Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana).
The Elastic Stack provides everything we need to build a powerful logging pipeline:
Filebeat (or Elastic Agent) ships i d x _ e 1 9 f 9 9 0 b logs from our containers or hosts
Logstash can i d x _ 1 6 4 a c c e 6 process, transform, and enrich logs before storing them
Elasticsearch acts i d x _ d 4 8 8 a 2 2 9 as the central search and analytics engine
Kibana i d x _ 1 e 5 d 6 f 9 4 gives us a user-friendly interface to query and visualize logs
Together, these components allow us to ship logs from many containers into one place, make them searchable in
near real time, and build dashboards that provide insights into system health and application behavior.
Note that the following description applies to a Linux system. If you happen to be one of the lucky people running
Linux natively on your developer machine, then go for it and start right away with Step 1a – setting up the ELK Stack
on Linux.
If, on the other hand, you are using a Mac or Windows machine for work, then we have created some step-by-step
instructions on how to test the setup. Of special notice is Step 1b – installing and configuring Filebeat. See the part
that matches your setup and give it a try.
Step 1a – Setting up the ELK Stack on Linux
Deploy Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana using Docker containers or install them directly on your i d x _ a 3 e b 2 1 9 9 system. For
detailed instructions, refer to the official i d x _ a a d 5 b e 7 3 ELK Stack documentation: https://www.elastic.co/docs.
Ensure that Elasticsearch and Kibana are properly configured and running. Verify this by accessing the Kibana
dashboard through a web browser.

Step 1b – Installing and configuring Filebeat
Filebeat is a lightweight log shipper that forwards logs from your Docker containers to the ELK Stack. Install
Filebeat on the Docker host machine and configure it to collect container logs:
Install Filebeat i d x _ 4 4 f 7 0 a 1 f using the official i d x _ 1 b 5 2 d d 2 e installation guide for your specific operating system. You can find the

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition

docs here: https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/beats/filebeat/current/filebeat-installation-
configuration.html.
Configure Filebeat by editing the filebeat.yml configuration file (usually located in /etc/filebeat on
Linux systems). Add the following configuration to collect Docker container logs:
filebeat.inputs:
- type: container
paths:
- '/var/lib/docker/containers/*/*.log'
Set up the output to forward logs to Elasticsearch. Replace <elasticsearch_host> and
<elasticsearch_port> with the appropriate values:
output.elasticsearch:
hosts: ["<elasticsearch_host>:<elasticsearch_port>"]
Save the configuration file and start Filebeat:
$ sudo systemctl enable filebeat
$ sudo systemctl start filebeat
Note that this setup is strictly for Linux systems. On Mac or Windows, the i d x _ e 6 7 f d d a 3 situation is i d x _ 0 7 f 4 f 9 9 f slightly more complicated,
given the fact that Docker runs in a VM on both systems, and as such, accessing the Docker logs that live inside this
VM is slightly more involved. Please consult the documentation if you want to install Filebeat natively on your Mac
or Windows machine, as this is outside the scope of this book. You can find exact instructions here: https://
www.elastic.co/docs/reference/beats/filebeat/filebeat-installation-configuration.
Alternatively, we can run Filebeat in a container, side by side with the Elastic Stack.

For now, we're going to learn how we can ship Docker daemon logs.
Shipping Docker daemon logs
Docker daemon logs i d x _ 3 c e 0 c 3 c 5 pertain to the overall functioning of the Docker platform. The Docker daemon is responsible
for managing all Docker containers, and its logs record system-wide events and messages. These logs help in
identifying issues related to the Docker daemon itself, such as networking problems, resource allocation errors, and
container orchestration challenges.
Depending on the operating system, the location and configuration of Docker daemon logs may differ. For
instance, on a Linux system, daemon logs are usually found in /var/log/docker.log, while on Windows, they are
located in %programdata%\docker\logs\daemon.log.
To effectively manage Docker daemon logs, consider the following best practices:
Regularly review daemon logs to identify potential issues and anomalies
Set up log rotation i d x _ e a 6 b 3 3 0 f and retention policies to manage disk space usage
Use a log management system to centralize and analyze logs for better visibility into the overall Docker
environment
In conclusion, both shipping containers and Docker daemon logs play vital roles in monitoring and maintaining a
healthy Docker environment. By effectively managing these logs, system administrators and developers can ensure
optimal performance, minimize downtime, and resolve issues promptly.

Docker daemon logs on Mac
On a Mac with Docker i d x _ e 9 1 d 1 e 4 5 Desktop installed, you can view the i d x _ 4 4 e 3 4 5 4 7 Docker daemon logs using the log stream command
provided by the macOS log utility. Follow these steps:
Open the Terminal application.
Run the following command:
$ sudo log stream --predicate 'senderImagePath \
CONTAINS "Docker"'
You must be an admin to run the log stream command. This command will display a real-time stream of
logs related to Docker Desktop, including the Docker daemon logs. You can stop the stream by pressing
Ctrl + C.
Alternatively, you can use the following command to view the Docker daemon logs in a file format:

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 390
chunks.content:
$ sudo log show --predicate 'senderImagePath \
CONTAINS "Docker"' \
--style syslog --info \
--last 1d > docker_daemon_logs.log
This command creates a file named docker_daemon_logs.log in the current directory, containing the
Docker daemon logs from the last day. You can change the --last 1d option i d x _ a 4 a 4 a 9 9 4 to specify a different time
i d x _ 0 9 8 8 b 8 2 0 range (for example, --last 2h for the last two hours). Open the docker_daemon_logs.log file with any
text editor to view the logs.
Please note that you may need administrator privileges to execute these commands. If you encounter permission
issues, prepend the commands with sudo.
Docker daemon logs on a Windows computer
On a Windows 11 machine i d x _ c f b c f b c 2 with Docker Desktop i d x _ b e e 2 3 e 9 d installed, the Docker daemon logs are stored as text files. You can
access these logs by following these steps:
Open File Explorer.
Navigate to the following directory:
C:\ProgramData\DockerDesktop\service
In this directory, you'll find the DockerDesktopVM.log file, which contains the Docker daemon logs.
Open the DockerDesktopVM.log file with any text editor to view the logs.
Please note that the C:\ProgramData folder might be hidden by default. To display hidden folders in File
Explorer, click on the View tab and check the Hidden items checkbox.

Next, we are i d x _ 3 8 4 a 4 0 1 b going i d x _ c 7 3 a 4 d 5 6 to learn how to query a centralized log.
Querying a centralized log with Kibana
When working with i d x _ 0 e a e a 2 3 8 multiple containerized applications, keeping track of their logs can quickly become
overwhelming. Each container writes its logs to its own output stream, making it hard to correlate events, track
failures, or see the big picture.
In production environments, logs are almost always sent to a centralized logging system. This allows engineers to
query, search, and visualize logs from all applications in one place, usually with tools such as Elasticsearch and
Kibana.
In this lab, you'll run two i d x _ 0 5 6 3 3 0 f c services, a Node.js API and i d x _ 6 2 1 a 0 9 7 0 a Ruby worker, that write logs to a shared Docker volume.
Filebeat tails the log files from that volume and ships them to Elasticsearch, where you'll query them with Kibana.
This is the exact pattern you use on macOS/Windows, where Docker runs inside a VM and /var/lib/docker/
containers isn't directly accessible.
By the end of this i d x _ 3 f 6 0 1 e 5 3 exercise, you'll know how to do the following:
Run a basic Elastic Stack (Elasticsearch + Kibana + Filebeat)
Collect logs from multiple containers automatically
Search and filter logs using Kibana's Discover view
Understand key fields such as container.name, log.level, and @timestamp

Step 3 – Creating the Ruby worker
The Ruby worker i d x _ 7 b c c a 9 7 e will i d x _ b 6 0 6 3 0 a c continuously print log lines, simulating a background process. Add a ruby-worker/
worker.rb file and add this content to it:

sleep 5

Similar to the Node.js API, the Ruby worker needs an entrypoint script. Add a ruby-worker/entrypoint.sh file
with this content:

mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LOGGING_FILE")"

Step 10 – Filtering and searching
Over time, an i d x _ f f e b 8 0 5 b application can create a massive amount of log entries. Luckily, we have powerful means to query
and filter logs in Kibana.
To show only Node.js logs, enter the following:
service.name : "node-api"
To search for errors, enter the following:
message : "ERROR"
To find logs from the last 15 minutes, use the time range selector in the top-right corner.
You can combine filters using AND/OR operators, such as the following:
service.name : "node-api" AND message : "ERROR"
Step 11 – Visualizing and saving
Once you've found i d x _ 3 4 1 1 e 5 1 7 interesting queries, you can create visualizations:
From the menu, choose Visualize Library | Create visualization.
Choose Lens as the visualization type.
Drag @timestamp to the x axis and Records to the y axis.
Use a filter such as container.name: node-api.
This quickly shows you log frequency over time, useful for spotting error bursts.
